feedback: When the child retells the story and names what is asked before computing, affirm that move explicitly: that understanding-first step is the goal.
If the child blurts a number, the partner does not accept it yet — it asks 'what is happening?' and 'how could you show that with your counters?'
When the child catches an unanswerable story ('that doesn't make sense, you can't work that out!'), the partner delights in the catch — this is the target moment.
Always close solvable stories with 'does your answer make sense in the story?' to plant the reasonableness habit.
activities.intendedInsight: A word problem is a situation to understand, not just numbers to do a sum with; sense-making and a reasonableness check come before and after calculating.
learnerActions: Listen to a tiny within-10 spoken story from a friendly partner character, e.g. 'Three frogs were on a log and two more hopped on.'
Before giving any answer, retell the story in your own words and say what is being asked ('what are we trying to find out?').
Show the story with counters/frogs or fingers ('show me with your frogs') so the part-part-whole structure is visible.
Work out an answer for a solvable story, then answer the partner's closing question: 'Does your answer make sense in the story?'
When the partner occasionally tells a deliberately silly story ('...so what colour is the pond?' or '...so how old is the cat?'), catch that it cannot be worked out and say why.
activities.title: The thinking partner who won't take a number yet

feedback: Accept justifications grounded in the story ('she gave some away so it must be fewer'); gently redirect answers that only restate a computation.
If the child says 'more' is possible after giving away, re-enact with counters to show that, when she only gives stickers away and gets none, the number she has can only go down.
activities.intendedInsight: Reasonableness is judged by the situation, so an answer can be ruled out before or without recomputing.
learnerActions: Given a within-10 story and a candidate answer, decide whether the answer could be right and explain why or why not.
For example: 'Maya has 6 stickers and gives some away. Could she end up with MORE than 6 stickers? How do you know?'
Explain using the situation ('fewer than 6 because she gave some away'), not by re-doing the sum.
activities.title: Single reasonableness check (which answer could not be right?)
